blocks.text: 1. Self-RAG

blocks.alt: A query goes through a model producing reflection tokens

blocks.text: Corrective RAG closed by contrasting its narrow grading approach with a broader form of self-correction. Self-RAG, where a model reflects on its own retrieval and generation decisions, is that broader form.
It decides whether to retrieve at all, then critiques its own generated answer, a reflective technique explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Deciding Whether To Retrieve At All

blocks.alt: A query is checked for whether to retrieve or not

blocks.text: Naive RAG's four stage pipeline always retrieves before generating, regardless of whether the query actually needs it.
Self-RAG first decides whether retrieval is even necessary for this specific query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pipeline","Retrieval decision"],"rows":[["Naive RAG","Always retrieves before generating"],["Self-RAG","Decides per query whether retrieval is needed"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Reflection Tokens Guide The Model
The model is trained to emit special reflection tokens marking its own decisions inline.
These tokens mark things such as whether retrieval is needed or whether a passage is relevant.
4. Critiquing Retrieved Passage Relevance

blocks.alt: A retrieved passage goes through self-critique to produce a relevance judgment

blocks.text: Self-RAG scores each retrieved passage for relevance inline during generation, echoing the grading Corrective RAG applies to retrieved chunks.
The difference is that this happens inline, rather than as a separate grading step run beforehand.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Unlike corrective RAG's separate grading pass before generation, self-RAG folds that same relevance judgment directly into the generation process itself through its trained reflection tokens.

blocks.text: 5. Critiquing Its Own Generated Answer

blocks.alt: A generated answer goes through self-critique to produce a quality judgment

blocks.text: Beyond grading retrieval, self-RAG also critiques whether the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved passage.
This adds a second layer of self-correction beyond just the input side.
6. Scoring Overall Response Quality
A final reflection step scores the overall usefulness of the complete response.
This allows multiple candidate generations to be compared and the best one selected.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Reflection point","What it evaluates"],"rows":[["Retrieval decision","Whether retrieval is needed at all"],["Passage relevance","Whether each retrieved passage is useful"],["Answer support","Whether the answer is grounded in the passage"],["Overall quality","Whether the complete response is useful"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Requires Training Not Just Prompting

blocks.alt: Prompting only is compared against a trained model

blocks.text: Much like the contrast between few-shot and zero-shot prompting in Few-Shot Prompting, self-RAG's reflection tokens require the model itself to be trained on that behavior.
This is unlike CRAG's grading step, which can be layered on top of any existing model.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Because self-RAG's reflection tokens are learned during training, adopting self-RAG means fine-tuning or using a model already trained this way, not simply writing a clever prompt.

blocks.text: 8. Self-RAG Versus CRAG

blocks.alt: Self-RAG has the model self-critique while CRAG uses a separate grader model

blocks.text: CRAG adds an external grading module around a fixed model, while self-RAG bakes reflection directly into the model itself.
This makes self-RAG a deeper but less portable form of self-correction.
9. Recognizing When Self-RAG Is Worth Its Training Requirement

blocks.alt: Being able to train a custom model points toward self-RAG

blocks.text: Teams able to fine-tune their own model can adopt self-RAG's deeper reflection.
Teams using a fixed, third-party model, by contrast, are better served by CRAG's external grading layer.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming self-RAG can be added through prompting alone without any model training.
Always retrieving regardless of query type, missing the retrieval decision self-RAG makes explicit.
Skipping the answer support check and only validating passage relevance.
Choosing self-RAG over CRAG when using a fixed third-party model that cannot be fine-tuned.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Self-RAG trains a model to reflect on its own retrieval and generation decisions.
It first decides whether retrieval is even necessary for a given query.
Trained reflection tokens mark decisions like retrieval necessity and passage relevance inline.
Passage relevance is critiqued inline during generation, not as a separate grading pass.
The generated answer is also critiqued for whether it is actually supported by the passage.
A final reflection step scores overall response quality across candidate generations.
Self-RAG requires training the model itself, unlike CRAG which layers grading externally.
Self-RAG suits teams that can fine-tune their own model; CRAG suits fixed third-party models.
